set1.io: d — Components of the pretest, intratest and posttest phases

That is listed under primary care.
Cholesterol
That is listed under primary care.

That is listed under primary care.

That describes non-instrumental point-of-care testing.

set2.io: l — Accreditation and regulatory considerations
set2.q: Which category describes slide examination of a freshly collected specimen by a provider, such as a Gram stain or manual cell count?
opts: Moderately complex testing
That category is usually automated.
Highly complex testing
That category involves complex instrumentation such as cross match testing.
Provider-performed microscopy
Correct — a distinct complexity category.
Waived testing
Waived testing is defined by low risk from an incorrect result.

set2.io: d — Components of the pretest, intratest and posttest phases
set2.q: What does the integration component of the posttest phase refer to?
opts: Reconciling the result against the pretest probability
That is a separate concept from the integration phase.
Diagnosis, subsequent acceptance, healing, and health-promoting behavior
Correct — it includes patient education for the diagnosis and treatment plan.
Combining results from several laboratories into a single unified record
Integration here refers to the patient's process, not to data merging.
Entering results into the electronic health record
That is documentation rather than integration.

set2.io: d — Components of the pretest, intratest and posttest phases
set2.q: Which principle is stated about documentation in the posttest phase?
opts: Verbal handoff is sufficient when the result is communicated directly
Detailed documentation is described as essential.
“If it wasn't documented, it wasn't done”
Correct — detailed documentation is described as essential to accurate record keeping and reporting.
Documentation may be deferred until results are final
Detailed documentation is expected rather than deferred.
Only abnormal results require documentation
Accurate record keeping applies regardless of the result.

set2.io: j — Availability, advantages and limitations of point-of-care testing
set2.q: Which is listed as an advantage of point-of-care testing?
opts: Greater precision than the equivalent central laboratory method in every case
Results may be less precise, which is listed as a limitation.
Lower cost than central laboratory testing
Expense is listed among the limitations.
Standardised vocabulary across manufacturers
Vocabulary is described as not always standardised, which is a limitation.
Better care where resources are limited, such as rural settings or disaster zones

set2.io: b — Patient counseling for diagnostic testing to reduce medical errors

The list is broader than education alone.
Only whether an interpreter is required
Language access matters but is not the full list.
Only the urgency of the clinical situation
Urgency does not replace individualised communication.
Ethnicity, culture, gender and age
Correct — these are named alongside preparing the patient properly and following standards.

set2.q: A state enacts laboratory regulation that differs from the federal Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments. What is the relationship?
opts: Federal regulation applies only where no state rule exists
The federal standard applies as the minimum everywhere.
State regulation applies only to hospital laboratories
The federal minimum applies to all testing sites.
State and city regulation will always be stricter, because the federal standard is the minimum and cannot be downgraded
Correct — states may add requirements but may never relax them.

States cannot downgrade the federal minimum.

set2.io: m — Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value
set2.q: What does incorporating prevalence into sensitivity produce?
opts: The pre-test probability applying to the next patient who is tested
Pre-test probability is an input rather than the output.
The clinically useful positive predictive value, by way of Bayes' theorem
Correct — moving from a test-centered probability to a patient-centered one.
The specificity of the test in that population
Specificity is a property of the test and does not derive from prevalence.
The incidence of the condition
Incidence is how often something happens, and is not derived this way.

Requiring two operators to witness each result

Repeating every abnormal result in the central laboratory

Chest percussion alone, without any aerosol

A prolonged breath hold before coughing

Delaying collection until the following morning
